profiles.name: Julie Bannon
profiles.excerpt: Julie Bannon was one of Lux Radio Theatre’s recurring studio voices, moving between dramatic performance and the sponsor material woven directly into the anthology.
profiles.bio_html:
Julie Bannon is a strong example of the radio professional whose surviving credits reveal more than surviving publicity. Golden Radio Hour’s detailed records place her repeatedly inside Lux Radio Theatre, where a large weekly company supported Hollywood guest stars and also helped deliver the sponsor material surrounding the drama.

Lux commercials were not always isolated announcements. Cast members could appear in conversational demonstrations, testimonials or short dramaticized sales passages, which meant a performer had to shift from fictional character to sponsor presentation without making the hour feel broken in two.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 52 Lux Radio Theatre credits for Bannon across performer and commercial-spokeswoman tags. Until stronger personal sources emerge, GRH treats that sustained studio record as the central fact of her radio career rather than inventing a fuller life story.

profiles.name: Joan Bennett
profiles.excerpt: Joan Bennett carried a major film career into radio drama and, on Suspense, also into the sponsor-facing performance that made commercial broadcasting possible.
profiles.bio_html:
Joan Bennett came from a theatrical family and became a major Hollywood actress whose screen career stretched from ingénue roles into the darker, more complex women of films directed by Fritz Lang. Radio repeatedly used that established screen identity, especially on prestige anthologies that could advertise a broadcast around a recognizable Hollywood name.

Her radio appearances included Lux Radio Theatre, Suspense and comedy-variety programs. GRH’s detailed records also tag two Suspense appearances with commercial-spokeswoman work, a reminder that even major stars could be drawn directly into the sponsor presentation rather than leaving all advertising to a staff announcer.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves four Lux Radio Theatre performances, two Suspense sponsor-tagged appearances, two Duffy’s Tavern appearances and additional work on Gunsmoke, Old Gold Comedy Theater and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar. GRH treats the commercial work as a secondary radio facet within a career defined primarily by acting.

profiles.name: Margaret Brayton
profiles.excerpt: Margaret Brayton was a busy West Coast radio actress whose Lux Radio Theatre work repeatedly crossed into sponsor presentation, alongside roles in mystery, comedy and literary drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Margaret Brayton belongs to the large Los Angeles repertory community that made weekly network drama possible. Her surviving GRH credits extend well beyond one program, including mystery, comedy and university-style literary adaptations, but Lux Radio Theatre is the clearest center of her archive record.

At Lux, Brayton appears under both performer and commercial-spokeswoman tags. That combination reflects the practical flexibility expected from studio actors on a sponsored anthology: a supporting player could help populate the drama and then participate in the sponsor segment built into the same live hour.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 41 Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits, seven NBC University Theater performances, four The Whistler appearances and smaller roles on Dr. Christian, Fibber McGee and Molly, Let George Do It, Screen Directors Playhouse and The Great Gildersleeve. GRH keeps the biography centered on that verified working-radio career.

profiles.name: Rosemary De Camp
profiles.excerpt: Rosemary DeCamp built her national reputation as Nurse Judy Price on Dr. Christian, then carried the same warm authority into film, television and sponsor-integrated radio work.
profiles.bio_html:
Rosemary DeCamp came to radio after stage work and became nationally known in 1937 as Judy Price, Dr. Paul Christian’s nurse and secretary on Dr. Christian. She remained identified with the role throughout the long-running series, giving the program an emotional and practical center beside Jean Hersholt’s country doctor.

Radio led directly into Hollywood. DeCamp moved into films in the early 1940s and later television, but she continued appearing on prestige radio anthologies such as Lux Radio Theatre. GRH’s Lux records include commercial-spokeswoman tags, showing that her trusted, familiar voice could also be used inside sponsor material.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 117 Dr. Christian performances, ten Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits and additional appearances on Academy Award Theater, Columbia Workshop, Old Gold Comedy Theater and The Shadow. Her page treats the sponsor work as one facet of a radio career anchored by Judy Price.

profiles.name: James Eagles
profiles.excerpt: James Eagles was a recurring Lux Radio Theatre studio actor whose archive record also preserves dozens of sponsor-facing credits alongside western, detective and anthology roles.
profiles.bio_html:
James Eagles is best documented through the surviving production record of West Coast radio. Golden Radio Hour places him repeatedly in Lux Radio Theatre, where supporting actors had to fit around major Hollywood guest stars and the complicated commercial structure of a live sponsored hour.

Eagles also worked on Dr. Christian, Philip Marlowe, Crime Classics, Gunsmoke, Rocky Fortune and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar. That spread shows a repertory actor comfortable moving among domestic drama, crime, westerns and anthology work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 61 Lux Radio Theatre commercial-spokesman/performer credits plus the additional dramatic appearances above. Reliable personal biography remains scarce, so GRH uses that unusually large verified Lux record as the center of his page.

profiles.name: Charles Emerson
profiles.excerpt: Charles Emerson was one of Lux Radio Theatre’s recurring supporting voices, appearing repeatedly in the dramatic and sponsor-facing work required by the weekly Hollywood anthology.
profiles.bio_html:
Charles Emerson survives in GRH primarily through Lux Radio Theatre credits rather than through a large body of publicity or later celebrity. That makes his record useful precisely because it documents the working studio company behind the famous guest stars.

Lux depended on supporting performers for small dramatic parts, crowd scenes, transitions and at times sponsor presentation. Emerson’s records carry both performer and commercial-spokesman roles, indicating that he was used on both sides of the boundary between story and sales message.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 19 Lux Radio Theatre credits for Emerson under those combined roles. GRH does not expand the page with unsupported personal detail; the repeated broadcast work is the strongest evidence currently available.

profiles.name: Stanley Farrar
profiles.excerpt: Stanley Farrar was a durable West Coast radio character actor whose Lux sponsor work sat beside recurring comedy, western and dramatic roles across the 1940s and 1950s.
profiles.bio_html:
Stanley Farrar built a broad radio repertory career rather than one star-making signature part. His GRH record moves through The Great Gildersleeve, westerns, detective series and prestige anthologies, showing the kind of professional flexibility that kept Los Angeles radio casts supplied week after week.

Lux Radio Theatre is the largest single part of that record. Farrar appears there under both performer and commercial-spokesman tags, meaning his work could extend from supporting dramatic roles into the sponsor presentation surrounding the adaptation.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 34 Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits, 20 The Great Gildersleeve performances, seven Wild Bill Hickok appearances and additional work on Let George Do It, NBC University Theater, The Railroad Hour, Barrie Craig and Roy Rogers. GRH treats that range as the biography’s central story.

profiles.name: John Fee
profiles.excerpt: John Fee was a recurring Lux Radio Theatre studio performer whose surviving credits show the same working actor moving directly into sponsor presentation.
profiles.bio_html:
John Fee is preserved in GRH almost entirely through Lux Radio Theatre, which makes his profile less a celebrity biography than a record of studio labor. The anthology’s famous guest stars depended on a regular pool of supporting voices who could fill smaller roles, handle transitions and participate in commercial material.

Fee’s records carry both performer and commercial-spokesman tags. That is important because it shows how sponsored radio used actors as part of the sales presentation rather than maintaining a rigid line between the play and the advertising around it.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 15 Lux Radio Theatre credits for John Fee under those combined roles. With little dependable personal documentation available, GRH keeps the page focused on that verified recurring work.

profiles.name: Verna Felton
profiles.excerpt: Verna Felton made a mature, unmistakable character voice one of radio’s most useful instruments, then carried it into Disney animation while also participating in sponsor material on Lux and Dr. Christian.
profiles.bio_html:
Verna Felton entered show business as a child and became one of radio’s busiest character actresses long before animation made her voice familiar to later generations. Her husky, commanding delivery could become a fussy mother, formidable matron, comic antagonist or warm older woman with only small changes in rhythm and pitch.

Radio used that range everywhere. Felton played Dennis Day’s mother on The Jack Benny Program, Aunt Aggie on The Judy Canova Show, Blossom Blimp on The Sealtest Village Store and numerous characters on Lux Radio Theatre, The Red Skelton Show and The Great Gildersleeve. Disney later used the same voice for characters including the Fairy Godmother in Cinderella and the Queen of Hearts in Alice in Wonderland.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 38 Lux Radio Theatre commercial-spokesman/performer credits, 22 Red Skelton Show appearances, 12 Railroad Hour performances and additional roles across several major series. GRH therefore treats sponsor presentation as one part of a much larger radio character-acting career.

profiles.name: Kathleen Fitz
profiles.excerpt: Kathleen Fitz was a recurring Lux Radio Theatre supporting voice whose archive record also places her inside the sponsor presentation of one of radio’s largest dramatic showcases.
profiles.bio_html:
Kathleen Fitz is another member of the working studio company whose contribution is clearer in broadcast logs than in surviving publicity. Her name recurs in Lux Radio Theatre, where Hollywood stars were surrounded by experienced radio actors who could make small roles register quickly.

GRH’s detailed records also attach commercial-spokesman tags to Fitz’s Lux appearances. That does not make advertising her only profession, but it does show that she was trusted to cross from dramatic support into the sponsor material embedded in the same broadcast.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 24 Lux Radio Theatre sponsor/performer credits for Fitz. Until stronger personal sources are located, GRH keeps her profile source-honest and centered on that repeated work rather than padding it with uncertain biography.

profiles.name: Ross Forrester
profiles.excerpt: Ross Forrester was one of Lux Radio Theatre’s most frequently recurring studio voices, with more than seventy credits spanning supporting performance and sponsor presentation.
profiles.bio_html:
Ross Forrester is preserved in Golden Radio Hour as a particularly strong example of the regular company behind Lux Radio Theatre. While the anthology sold itself on Hollywood stars, every adaptation still required experienced radio actors for smaller parts, crowd work, transitions and the commercial segments built into the hour.

Forrester’s records repeatedly carry both performer and commercial-spokesman roles. The scale matters: this is not a stray sponsor tag attached to one broadcast, but a recurring pattern across years of Lux production.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 74 Lux Radio Theatre commercial-spokesman/performer credits for Ross Forrester. Personal biographical documentation remains limited, so GRH presents the sustained Lux relationship itself as the strongest verified evidence of his radio career.
